Dear Reviewer fhBo,

We really appreciate your comments. We hope our point-to-point response can address your concerns. The new guidelines prohibit changes to the manuscript or code at this stage, but we hope to update a few sections at a later time, if and when possible.

1. *"While the authors introduce ..."* : Thank you for this insightful comment. Our goal in generating a broad range of hood variants is to probe how geometric diversity influences fluid–structure response—and to furnish ML models with rich training data—rather than to propose immediately production-ready designs as detailed in the Sections 1 and 2. That said, we enforce several implicit manufacturability and plausibility constraints:
- *Minimum feature sizes and spacings*: All cutouts maintain a user-defined minimum distance from each other and from shell edges, avoiding undercuts or excessively thin walls.
- *Symmetric, planar cutouts*: By mirroring 2D profiles and projecting them onto a convex-hull shell of uniform thickness, we ensure no overhangs or draft‐angle violations, ensuring compatibility with stamping or extrusion processes.
- *Curvature and smoothness restrictions*: Profiles are Bézier-based and sampled at high resolution, preventing sharp corners that would be infeasible during manufacturing.

While a direct nearest-neighbor comparison against CarHoods10K could further validate our variants’ practicality, that dataset includes only inner-hood profiles, whereas our AutoHood3D provides full-shell geometries. We acknowledge this could be a valuable future enhancement for downstream engineering workflows.


2. *"Fig. 2 illustrates the ..."* : The re-embedding workflow is fully detailed in Appendix C.3, and we have provided a reference implementation in the repository: please see 01_Generating_Hoods/02_Creating_Hoods_multiProc.py, which includes in-code documentation and a corresponding README listing all software dependencies and parameters. This script automatically fits each ordered point-cloud curve to the 3D shell surface (following user-defined center-plane offsets and minimum spacings) and performs the Boolean cutout operations directly on the base hood STL. 

3. *"The authors report ..."* : We restrict our quantitative ML experiments to a representative subset of ~4500 cases—stratified across all nine clusters and base shells—to balance thorough model evaluation with computational feasibility. Training on all 16000 samples would demand roughly ten times more GPU hours and I/O bandwidth—and may mask true architectural differences by mixing data‐scale effects with model behavior. Our chosen subset of 4500 points preserves the full spectrum of geometric and FSI behaviors, ensuring that conclusions about model performance generalize across the dataset. The complete 16000-case dataset remains available for large-scale training or application-specific studies, and we have include PyTorch scripts to train on the entire collection using data-distributed parallelism (DDP).

4. *"In Sec 3.3, the authors state the text ..."* : The automated text prompts are intended as an extension—demonstrating how AutoHood3D could underpin emerging Text-to-CAD workflows (e.g., Text2CAD)—but detailed benchmarking of text-to-geometry generation falls outside the core FSI and surrogate-model contributions of this work.
We believe that before tackling a full Text2CAD pipeline, it was essential to establish a parametrized, engineering-level geometry space (potentially involving up to 20 parameters) and generate the corresponding high-fidelity simulation data. Our prompts correspond to “Level 2” and “Level 3” descriptions as per Fig. 4 from Text2CAD article, which capture curve count, spacing, and symmetry, but we emphasize that more sophisticated surface-contour and conforming-language extensions will be needed to handle the complexity of real-world designs. Text descriptions are automatically generated from the hood metadata following the naming conventions in Fig. 11 (Appendix C.3) and self-validated by the model. We appreciate the suggestion of expert human review, that would further reduce errors, but this step is beyond the scope of the present work. Moreover, by open-sourcing our design-synthesis workflow, users can trace every geometric transformation and generate high-quality datasets for advanced mesh-generation challenges—such as long-sequence geometry editing and adaptive topology guided by natural-language prompts [1]. We plan to clarify in the manuscript that these annotations and workflows are intended to enable broader Text-to-CAD and mesh-learning research beyond the core FSI contributions.\
*References*\
[1] Hao, Zekun, et al. "Meshtron: High-fidelity, artist-like 3d mesh generation at scale." arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.09548 (2024).

5. *"The paper does not convincingly ..."* :  Although our pipeline can deterministically generate any hood variant, the paired text prompts provide a natural-language interface that: (1) empowers non-CAD-expert users to specify designs; (2) enables zero-shot or few-shot generative-AI workflows for rapid shape synthesis and editing; and (3) aligns with real-world requirements that originate as textual specifications, thereby bridging upstream design intent to automated CAD generation. While the text prompts are not the core focus of this study, they serve as an optional extension to demonstrate how our dataset can support natural-language interfaces and generative-AI workflows, complementing—but not replacing—the primary parametric pipeline. 

We appreciate your thoughtful feedback and hope that, with these clarifications, you will reassess our manuscript and reconsider its suitability for publication.

Dear Reviewer xbCd,

We really appreciate your comments and your support for our work. We hope our response adequately addresses your concerns. 
Please find our detailed response below. The new guidelines prohibit changes to the manuscript or code, but we hope to update a few sections at a later time, if and when possible.

1. *"The cutouts in the hood ..."* : Thank you for this thoughtful comment. We agree that purely 2D segmentation can, in theory, miss subtle surface undulations and over-hanging features that a full 3D approach might capture. However, our pipeline employs several strategies to preserve true 3D geometry: \
**Shell Reconstruction via Convex Hull and Offset**\
Before any cutout is applied, we compute the convex hull of the original inner-hood mesh and offset it to form the complete exterior shell. This step retains all three-dimensional surface contours—including curvature normals—ensuring that the subsequent cutout region fully conforms to the actual hood topology.\
**Back-Projection of 2D Masks onto the 3D Surface**\
Following 2D segmentation with SAM-2, each mask boundary is reprojected onto the high‐resolution 3D mesh. This back-projection is analogous to the multi-view fusion techniques used in projective shape segmentation, which have been shown to yield coherent 3D labels by aggregating 2D predictions across views [1] . Consequently, our cutouts conform exactly to the shell’s curvature and local topology.\
**High-Resolution Sampling**\
We uniformly sample each mask contour with 100+ boundary points and perform Boolean subtraction directly on the 3D mesh, avoiding interpolation artifacts. This approach mirrors the practices of state-of-the-art mesh-based segmentation frameworks—such as MeshSegmenter (based on SAM) [2]—that leverage high-resolution contours to preserve geometric detail in segmented regions.

While true volumetric 3D segmentation (e.g., using 3D U-Nets) could capture undercuts and overhangs, it often incurs prohibitive computational costs and requires volumetric ground truth that is unavailable (CarHoods10K only contains inner hood geometry) for our application. Our approach strikes a balance by leveraging the efficiency of 2D segmentation and the fidelity of 3D re-projection—an approach widely adopted in graphics and vision research for efficient yet accurate 3D part delineation [3]. In future work, we plan to integrate advanced CAD operations for even finer surface features for specific use cases in our open-source pipeline. For now, we believe our current pipeline provides a practical, high-throughput solution that maintains the critical three-dimensional characteristics of the hood shell and cutouts.

*References*\
[1] Wang, Yunhai, et al. "Projective analysis for 3D shape segmentation." ACM Transactions on Graphics (TOG) 32.6 (2013): 1-12.\
[2] Zhong, Ziming, et al. "Meshsegmenter: Zero-shot mesh semantic segmentation via texture synthesis." European Conference on Computer Vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.\
[3] Garosi, Marco, et al. "3d part segmentation via geometric aggregation of 2d visual features." 2025 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV). IEEE, 2025.

2. *"ML benchmarking is ..."* : Thank you for this comment. As mentioned in the rebuttal to Reviewer 5BZ6, we agree that our benchmark models - MLP, PointNet, GraphSAGE, Graph U-Net, and PointGNNConv have newer variants. However, our data loaders and data format (point cloud and STL) readily support newer architectures—including SE(3)-equivariant GNNs (EGNN [1], PaiNN [2]), transformer-based point models (PointTransformer [3], Graphormer [4]), and neural operators (FNO [5], GNO [6])—as well as spatio-temporal extensions for sequence modeling. 

3. *"The paper includes natural ..."* : Thank you for this observation. While we provide structured natural-language prompts paired with each geometry, we do not include benchmark results for text-to-geometry synthesis in the current manuscript. Our primary focus here is the generation and validation of the FSI dataset and surrogate-model baselines. That said, we agree that evaluating LLMs and vision-language models on the prompt-to-point-cloud task is both important and timely. Developing a comprehensive benchmark for multi-modal architectures (e.g., PointLLM [1], MeshAnything v2 [2], etc.)—complete with quantitative metrics and qualitative case studies—requires substantial effort and falls outside the scope of this work. Nevertheless, we believe the provided prompts and code offer a robust foundation for the community to build upon and conduct meaningful evaluations.\
*References*\
[1] Xu, Runsen, et al. "Pointllm: Empowering large language models to understand point clouds." European Conference on Computer Vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.\
[2] Chen, Yiwen, et al. "Meshanything v2: Artist-created mesh generation with adjacent mesh tokenization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2408.02555 (2024).

Thank you for helping us strengthen our work.

Users can specify arbitrary flow incidence angles or even impose rotational impulses about the hood surface. The entire generation pipeline is open-source, so the community can readily create new boundary-condition configurations for specific use cases.   


2. *"MLP performs so much better than..."* :Thank you for this insightful question. We agree that our MLP’s hidden‐layer width is four times the dimensionality of its encoder output—in our case a 64 to 256 configuration—but this does not directly imply that the MLP is aggregating information from four neighboring points. Rather, each vertex’s feature vector (comprised of its coordinates, normals and distance field) is processed independently through fully connected layers, without explicit pooling or message passing over spatial neighbors. The unexpectedly strong in-distribution performance of the MLP therefore cannot be directly attributed to local geometric aggregation in the same way as graph models. To investigate this further, we performed the following studies:

**Hypotheses and Tests**

|                Hypothesis               | Description                                                                     | Result                                                                                                     |
| :-------------------------------------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|           A. **Non-homophily**          | If adjacent nodes differ greatly, graph aggregation may harm performance.       | **Rejected**: high homophily found (see Table 1), so GNNs should benefit from local pooling.               |
| B. **Sensitivity to neighbor count ($m_{\mathrm{NN}}$)** | GraphSAGE performance depends on neighborhood size.                             | **Confirmed**: larger $m_{\mathrm{NN}}$ reduces prediction error but at steep compute and I/O cost.                   |
|    C. **MLP Capacity & Overfitting**    | The wide MLP memorizes training-set patterns, inflating in-distribution scores. | **Supported**: ablation shows ID error rises with hidden-dim reduction while OOD error improves (Table below). |


A. ***Homophily Test***\
The hood surface often exhibits cutout edges and curvature changes that could cause non-homophily. In such cases, neighborhood pooling of GNNs can oversmooth fine features—whereas an MLP’s point-wise mapping avoids this [1], potentially explaining its ID test errors. Therefore, to measure the non-homophily, we computed numeric assortativity ( $\bar{r}$ ) [2] and a standard edge-wise multi-dimensional cosine similarity [3] over the entire in-distribution test data/graphs:
|         Field        |   $\bar {r}$  | $\sigma_r$ |
| :------------------: | :---------: | :--------: |
|           Ux          |   +0.9756   |   0.0037   |
|           Uy          |   +0.9739   |   0.0106   |
|           Uz          |   +0.9711   |   0.0059   |
|           p          |   +0.9650   |   0.0058   |
|           Dx          |   +0.9910   |   0.0301   |
|           Dy        |   +0.9933   |   0.0154   |
|           Dz          |   +0.9877   |   0.0322   |
| **Multi-dim Cosine** | +0.9449 | 0.0109 |

Interpretation: All fields exhibit strong homophily ( $\bar{r}$ > 0.96), so neighbor aggregation should be beneficial for GNNs—not detrimental—if effectively leveraged. This can be done by carefully selecting the "max neighbors" (mNN), as the quality of feature aggregation in GNNs is significantly influenced by this choice. This is the focus of Test B, where we explore the impact of mNN selection on GNN performance in more detail.

B. ***GraphSAGE $m_{\mathrm{NN}}$ Sweep***\
In a separate experiment (see Appendix A.1 Table 6), we varied GraphSAGE’s neighbor count (mNN = 4,8,16,32). Increasing the neighborhood size from 4 to 32 reduces ID MSE by up to 40-50%, but:\
*Compute Time*: per-epoch time grows by an order of magnitude.\
*Data I/O*: dataset size inflates proportionally to neighborhood features stored.\
Higher mNN reduced in-distribution errors at the expense of increased computation time, illustrating the classic trade-off of neighborhood aggregation.

C. ***MLP Hidden-Size Ablation Study***\
Our ablation study compared MLPs with hidden‐layer widths of 256, 128 and 64—keeping all other hyperparameters consistent with Table 5. Below are selected set of results for brevity:
|    Model    | $D_x$ ID MSE $(10^{-2})$ | $D_x$ OOD MSE $(10^{-2})$ |
| :---------: | :----------------------: | :-----------------------: |
| **MLP 256** |           2.80           |           181.02           |
| **MLP 128** |           4.59           |           175.28           |
| **MLP 064** |           7.63           |           124.11           |

ID Trend: error increases steeply as hidden dimension shrinks, confirming that the 256-dim model leverages high capacity to fit training data.\
OOD Trend: the smaller MLPs generalize *marginally* better, indicating the largest network is more susceptible to overfitting the data.\
Here is the complete set of results: \
*In-Distribution Results (MSE × 10$^{-2}$)* 
| Model   | Ux   | Uy   | Uz   | P    | Dx   | Dy   | Dz   |
| ------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| MLP 256 | 0.25 | 0.27 | 0.44 | 0.37 | 2.80 | 0.51 | 0.76 |
| MLP 128 | 0.32 | 0.30 | 0.49 | 0.47 | 4.59 | 0.75 | 0.91 |
| MLP 064 | 0.39 | 0.37 | 0.53 | 0.58 | 7.63 | 0.74 | 1.02 |

*Out-Distribution Results (MSE × 10$^{-2}$)*
| Model   | Ux   | Uy   | Uz   | P    | Dx     | Dy   | Dz    |
| ------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ------ | ---- | ----- |
| MLP 256 | 1.49 | 1.89 | 2.97 | 4.96 | 181.02 | 5.87 | 19.81 |
| MLP 128 | 1.58 | 1.60 | 2.68 | 4.65 | 175.28 | 7.58 | 22.91 |
| MLP 064 | 2.14 | 1.09 | 1.59 | 3.38 | 124.11 | 8.50 | 20.55 |

Together, these studies indicate that:
 - MLP’s ID test advantage is not directly due to hidden neighbor aggregation—its wider layers enable point-wise memorization of global patterns.
 - Graph models exploit the existing homophily but must carefully balance neighborhood size against oversmoothing and computational overhead.
 - Practical surrogate design will therefore depend on application: MLPs for high-throughput, in-distribution tasks, and GNNs (with tuned mNN) for robust generalization where compute resources permit. We intend to incorporate these findings and explanations into the revised appendix of the manuscript in a future update.

*References*\
[1] Zhang, Shichang, et al. "Graph-less neural networks: Teaching old mlps new tricks via distillation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.08727 (2021).\
[2] Newman, Mark EJ. "Mixing patterns in networks." Physical review E 67.2 (2003): 026126. \
[3] Abu-El-Haija, Sami, et al. "Mixhop: Higher-order graph convolutional architectures via sparsified neighborhood mixing." international conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2019.

For the additional feedback - Thank you for this thoughtful perspective. We agree that a fully realized Text-to-CAD system will require a far richer variety of geometries and perhaps different representation formats (e.g., CSG trees). Our pipeline already performs a series of mesh‐level Boolean operations such as thickening, extrusion, subtract and mirror that mimic CSG workflows. What we don’t yet capture is an explicit, high-level CSG representation (with named primitives and operation nodes) that could be directly edited or composed via text. Our natural-language annotations are intended as a foundational step—demonstrating how structured prompts can map to complex, parametric hood shapes. Incorporating a highly-structured CSG metadata is an excellent direction for future extensions of AutoHood3D, especially to support "fully generative" Text-to-CAD workflows that integrates diverse CAD abstractions and larger geometry corpora.

Thank you for helping us strengthen our work.

rebuttal.value:
Dear Reviewer 5BZ6,

We really appreciate your thoughtful comments and your support for our work. We hope our response can address your concerns. 
Please find our detailed response below. The new guidelines prohibit changes to the manuscript or code at this stage, but we hope to update a few sections at a later time, if and when possible.

1. *"The description of the ML baselines is unclear... "*: Thank you for pointing this. Yes, we briefly describe the feature set in the manuscript, and we plan to expand upon the following in the manuscript later: \
**Inputs** \
Point-cloud mode: Per-vertex coordinates (x,y,z), signed‐distance, and normals concatenated into a 7-dimensional feature vector.
Graph-based mode: The same per-vertex features, plus edge_index computed via a fixed-radius neighbor search to define mesh connectivity.  \
**Outputs** \
Per-vertex targets comprising velocity components, scalar pressure, and displacement components. \
**Time Encoding** \
Each training example is a single quasi-steady “snapshot” at peak loading; we do not include a temporal sequence or explicit time feature in the input. However, we do provide temporal snapshots in the dataset for time-series analysis using emerging architectures. \
Although we benchmark MLP, PointNet, GraphSAGE, Graph U-Net, and PointGNNConv, our data loaders and Data(pos,x,y,edge_index) format (point clouds and STLs) readily support newer architectures—including SE(3)-equivariant GNNs (EGNN [1], PaiNN [2]), transformer-based point models (PointTransformer [3], Graphormer [4]), and neural operators (FNO [5], GNO [6])—as well as spatio-temporal extensions for sequence modeling. We have briefly discussed this in our future work section and intend to expand on this later. 

*References* \
[1] Liu, Zhaowei, et al. "EGNN: Graph structure learning based on evolutionary computation helps more in graph neural networks." Applied Soft Computing 135 (2023): 110040. \
[2] Schütt, Kristof, Oliver Unke, and Michael Gastegger. "Equivariant message passing for the prediction of tensorial properties and molecular spectra." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2021. \
[3] Zhao, Hengshuang, et al. "Point transformer." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF international conference on computer vision. 2021. \
[4] Lin, Kevin, Lijuan Wang, and Zicheng Liu. "Mesh graphormer." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF international conference on computer vision. 2021. \
[5] Kovachki, Nikola, et al. "Neural operator: Learning maps between function spaces with applications to pdes." Journal of Machine Learning Research 24.89 (2023): 1-97. \
[6] Eliasof, Moshe, Lars Ruthotto, and Eran Treister. "Improving graph neural networks with learnable propagation operators." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2023. 


2. *"The material properties are uniform..."* : Thank you for this important question. Applying uniform, isotropic material properties (e.g., aluminum‐alloy or steel-alloy stiffness [1]) is standard for baseline FSI studies of single-material components—such as the automotive hoods examined here—to isolate geometric influences on deformation under specified loading conditions. Importantly, this simplification does not diminish the dataset’s real-world relevance—it captures the fundamental load–deflection trends that inform component sizing, stress‐hotspot identification and initial design decisions regarding composite layups. 
Moreover, our framework supports advance models: OpenFOAM accommodates tensorial definitions for anisotropic/aeolotropic elasticity, and preCICE can couple with external solvers (e.g., solids4foam or deal.II) to simulate composite structure or targeted reinforcements in high-deflection regions. 

*References* \
[1] Lautrup, B. (2011). Physics of continuous matter: exotic and everyday phenomena in the macroscopic world. CRC press.


Thank you for helping us strengthen our work.

summary.value: AutoHood3D introduces the first large-scale, open-source benchmark focused on 3-D automotive hood design under fluid–structure interaction (FSI) loading. The authors generate more than 16 k hood geometries, each simulated with high-fidelity, one-way coupled LES–FEA to capture transient deformation caused by rotary-dip-paint fluid entrapment. The release includes multi-modal assets—STL meshes, time-resolved CFD/FEA fields, point clouds, and paired natural-language prompts—plus a fully reproducible pipeline (geometry synthesis, meshing, preCICE-based co-simulation). Baselines on five neural architectures (MLP, PointNet, GraphSAGE, Graph U-Net, PointGNNConv) quantify speed–accuracy trade-offs for predicting pressure and displacement, highlighting simple models’ in-distribution strengths and graph models’ out-of-distribution robustness. Overall, AutoHood3D provides a rich testbed for surrogate modeling, physics-informed learning, and text-to-geometry generative design while offering extensible tools for future 3-D multiphysics benchmarks.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.Comprehensive, high-fidelity FSI benchmark – 16 k+ 3-D hood geometries with time-resolved LES-FEA snapshots fill a clear gap in open multiphysics datasets and enable realistic surrogate-model research.
2. Rich multimodal release with reproducible pipeline – STL meshes, CFD/FEA fields, point clouds, and paired text prompts plus open-sourced generation and simulation scripts let others extend or adapt the dataset easily.
3. Rigorous baselines clarify speed-accuracy trade-offs – Five neural architectures are benchmarked for both in-distribution and OOD cases, giving actionable guidance for choosing between fast MLP/PointNet surrogates and more generalizable graph models.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The description of the ML baselines is unclear—please specify exactly what the model inputs and outputs are and how the time steps are encoded. Additionally, clarify whether more recent network architectures or other ML methods can be applied to this type of data.
2. The material properties are uniform across the mesh. Is this standard practice in the field, or could it limit the dataset’s real-world impact?

summary.value: The authors carefully curate a dataset of automotive hood geometries and run high fidelity multiphysics simulations on these geometries to calculate aerodynamic fluid forces and their resulting structural stresses on the hood. They build a custom pipeline to generate these geometries and run the simulation. They benchmark a number of models on the task of predicting fluid flow, pressure and displacement fields. They authors also extend the dataset with a collection of text prompts for the purposes of LLM finetuning for CAD problems.

strengths_contributions.value: Firstly I would like to thank the authors for their effort and attention to detail, the paper was very enjoyable to read, with good figures and clear descriptions of the work and problems involved. The provided dataset is high quality and well constructed, and the dataset generation pipeline is well thought out and very generalizable. All details of dataset construction and model training are clearly presented.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The paper is well structured and all information is clearly presented. There are not many weaknesses, though there are one or two small points which would be good to expand on.
- as far as I can tell, the fluid velocity is always directed perpendicularly to the hood surface. This makes sense for the problem described in the paper (relating to the painting of the hood), but feels like it limits the usability of the dataset for other similar problems. It would be nice to include more configurations of the fluid boundary conditions.
- I find it surprising that the MLP performs so much better than more structured models in the in distribution tests. Even in the out of distribution test, the MLP is still outperforming some of the graph based models on many of the field predictions. After looking through the appendix I see that the hidden size of the MLP model is 4× that of the encoder output, should I take that to mean that the MLP is operating on 4 neighbors at a time? If this is the case it would make more sense that the MLP can incorporate geometric information. If it is not incorporating any geometric information, then these results are suspicious to me and perhaps warrant further investigation of the models.

additional_feedback.value: While I do not consider this to be a negative point, I do find the use case of LLM - CAD fine-tuning to be somewhat unconvincing. There is certainly some value in providing this data, but I suspect a much larger variety of geometry and other CAD representations (CSG trees for example) would be necessary to make a useful text to CAD workflow. This data could be one small part of that, but I think it has limited scope in this use case.

final_justification.value: The paper is well written and high quality. The authors have addressed my point regarding the mlp performance, and performed further investigation into the behavior of the models and graph features. I recommend this paper for publication.

summary.value: The paper introduces AutoHood3D, a dataset with 16,000+ automotive hood designs for machine learning in engineering. It includes STL meshes, time-resolved physical fields, and natural language prompts for text-to-geometry synthesis. The dataset addresses gaps in existing ones and supports physics-aware ML and generative design. It also proposes multiphysics loss functions for improved model training and new FSI benchmarks.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper provides a fully reproducible, end-to-end pipeline that allows users to generate, simulate, and analyze automotive hood designs. This reproducibility is crucial for advancing research in automotive design optimization and FSI modeling, and it will likely promote further development in physics-aware ML.
2. The dataset's diverse formats make it suitable for a wide range of ML applications.
3.  The work is grounded in real manufacturing challenges.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The cutouts in the hood geometries are defined via 2D projections, which might overlook more intricate 3D features, potentially limiting representation of realistic, highly curved components.
2. ML benchmarking is limited to a few outdated models from before 2020, I think more recent techniques should be validated.
3. The paper includes natural language prompts for text-to-geometry synthesis but does not benchmark any models on this task.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

summary.value: The authors introduce AutoHood3D, a new multiphysics 3D dataset for automotive hood analysis. The dataset consists of 16K 3D hood mesh models, accompanied by detailed generation workflows. Specifically, 100 inner-only hood geometries from CarHoods10K are used as the base shell. To obtain diverse cutout patterns, 250 inner-hood geometries from CarHoods10K are further utilized. A total of 1,750 cutout variants are designed, and K-Means clustering is applied to group them into 7 distinct clusters, resulting in 16K final hood meshes. For computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation, OpenFOAM v2312 is employed, while text descriptions for the dataset are generated using Gemma3. Using the proposed dataset, the authors train multiple models, including MLP, PointNet, GraphSAGE, Graph U-Net^2, and PointGNNConv, to predict velocity components, pressure, and displacement. Experimental results indicate that simple model architectures, such as MLP and PointNet, achieve the best performance in in-distribution scenarios.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The authors present first large-scale, open-source multi-modal FSI benchmark for automotive design, while existing dataset are often confined to 2D cases and exhibit limited geometric diversity.

2. The dataset provides multiple complementary modalities essential for modern data-driven engineering.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. While the authors introduce a large number of synthetically generated automotive hood geometries, the practical motivation for such generation is not sufficiently justified. The generated geometries are produced via automated recombination of 2D cutout profiles onto base shell surfaces. It remains uncertain whether all generated geometries are physically plausible or manufacturable, limiting their utility for downstream engineering workflows. CarHoods10K shows the difference between optimized design and the closest design of automotive hood. Such a comparative analysis is particularly valuable, as it provides clear insight.

2. Fig. 2 illustrates the projection of the 3D hood surface onto a 2D plane, applying segmentation to obtain masks, and subsequently extracting curve boundaries. However, a detailed description of re-embedding step of ordered point cloud curve are missing. Does the accompanying software automatically performs cutouts directly from the point cloud?

3. The authors report the creation of a 16K data but then restrict their experimental evaluation to only 4.5K data. The justification for this significant subset selection is not provided.

4. In Sec 3.3, the authors state the text descriptions are generated automatically using the Gemma3 vision-language model based on geometric metadata. Without a demonstrated downstream use case, like Text2CAD[1], the practical utility of these text annotations remains unclear. Also, there is a lack of expert evaluations verifying whether the generated text descriptions accurately and consistently correspond to the associated geometries. 

5. The paper does not convincingly justify why text descriptions are essential given that hood geometries can already be generated deterministically via the explicit parametric pipeline outlined in Fig. 2.

[1] Khan et al., Text2CAD: Generating Sequential CAD Designs from Beginner-to-Expert Level Text Prompts, NeurIPS 2024

title.value: AutoHood3D: A Multi‑Modal Benchmark for Automotive Hood Design and Fluid–Structure Interaction

TLDR.value: AutoHood3D is a multi‑modal dataset of automotive hood variants—combining FSI simulations, STL meshes, natural‑language prompts, and standardized ML benchmarks—for generative engineering design and surrogate modeling.

abstract.value: This study presents a new high-fidelity multi-modal dataset containing 16000+ geometric variants of automotive hoods useful for machine learning (ML) applications such as engineering component design and process optimization, and multiphysics system surrogates. The dataset is centered on a practical multiphysics problem—hood deformation from fluid entrapment and inertial loading during rotary‑dip painting. Each hood is numerically modeled with a coupled Large-Eddy Simulation (LES)-Finite Element Analysis (FEA), using 1.2M cells in total to ensure spatial and temporal accuracy. The dataset provides time-resolved physical fields, along with STL meshes and structured natural language prompts for text-to-geometry synthesis. Existing datasets are either confined to 2D cases, exhibit limited geometric variations, or lack the multi‑modal annotations and data structures—shortcomings we address with AutoHood3D. We validate our numerical methodology, establish quantitative baselines across five neural architectures, and demonstrate systematic surrogate errors in displacement and force predictions. These findings motivate the design of novel approaches and multiphysics loss functions that enforce fluid–solid coupling during model training. By providing fully reproducible workflows, AutoHood3D enables physics‑aware ML development, accelerates generative‑design iteration, and facilitates the creation of new FSI benchmarks.
